summary: Specifies the process for selecting, confirming and recalling IAB and IESG members, including the operation of the Nominating and Recall Committees. It is a best current practice. It obsoletes RFC 2727, was updated by RFC 5078, RFC 5633, RFC 5680 and RFC 6859, and was replaced by RFC 7437.

eli5.summary: This is the rulebook for how volunteers pick the leaders of the internet's rule-making groups, and how to remove one if needed.

who confirms iab and iesg candidates
subtitle: The rulebook for how the IETF picks, confirms and, if needed, removes the members of its IAB and IESG.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs a fair, repeatable way to fill the seats on its architecture board (IAB) and steering group (IESG), and a way to remove a sitting member.
tldr.mechanism: A Nominating Committee of randomly chosen volunteers nominates candidates, a confirming body approves or rejects them, and a separate recall committee, built like the Nominating Committee, handles recalls.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3777 obsoleted RFC 2727 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 7437, after updates by RFC 5078, RFC 5633, RFC 5680 and RFC 6859.

today: RFC 3777 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 10) that has been obsoleted by RFC 7437, so it no longer describes the current process. Before that it was updated by RFC 5078, RFC 5633, RFC 5680 and RFC 6859, and it replaced RFC 2727.

sections.title: The Annual Cycle and Its Ground Rules
sections.content:
The yearly process has three parts: selecting and organizing the Nominating Committee members, selecting candidates, and confirming them. It is due to finish within 7 months, one month before the Friday of the week before the First IETF, with an extra month before new terms begin that can absorb unusual delays. Time frames are measured in IETF meetings, assuming three a year.

The committee reviews each open IESG and IAB position and either nominates the incumbent or a superior candidate. About one-half of each body's positions are reviewed every year, and confirmed candidates are expected to serve at least a 2 year term. All deliberations about specific nominees and candidates are confidential.

Confirmation uses an advice and consent model. The sitting IAB confirms IESG candidates, and the Internet Society Board of Trustees confirms IAB candidates. If a body has no decision rule of its own, confirming a candidate should need at least one-half of its sitting members to agree.

A mid-term vacancy is filled by the same rules with four changes: the current committee handles it (the prior year's committee during the overlap), it is due within 6 weeks, the confirming body has two weeks to reject a candidate or the candidate is assumed confirmed, and the new term is the remainder of the old one, or the remainder plus 2 years when less than a year is left.
sections.eli5: Every year about half of the leader seats are up for a new vote. One group suggests names, another group says yes or no, and everything said about the people stays secret.

sections.title: Who Sits on the Nominating Committee
sections.content:
The committee has at least a Chair, 10 voting volunteers, 3 liaisons and an advisor. The Internet Society President appoints the Chair. The IAB and the IESG each appoint a liaison from their own membership, someone not in an open position, and the Board of Trustees may appoint one. The prior year's Chair serves as an advisor and is expected to watch over the current Chair.

Only the voting volunteers vote on candidate selection. The Chair, liaisons and advisors do not, though they vote on other questions. A committee term is expected to last 15 months, overlapping the next committee's term by about three months.

The Chair is responsible for finishing the work on time and must attest at a plenary session of the First IETF that the results are the committee's best effort and in the best interests of the IETF community. Committee members are not eligible to fill the open positions of the committee they serve on.
sections.eli5: The committee is mostly ordinary volunteers who get to vote, plus helpers from the groups being picked who may talk but may not vote on the names.

sections.title: Choosing the Volunteers
sections.content:
The Chair announces the open positions and asks the community for volunteers, giving at least 30 days to respond. A volunteer must have attended at least 3 of the last 5 IETF meetings, and the IETF Secretariat checks this. Sitting IAB and IESG members and members of the Internet Society Board of Trustees may not volunteer.

The 10 voting volunteers are picked at random. The method must depend on random data that is not known until the selection date, must be fair (each eligible volunteer equally likely) and unbiased (no one can steer the result), must be independently verifiable and repeatable, and must produce an ordered list. RFC 3777 points to RFC 2777 as one possible method. No more than two volunteers with the same primary affiliation may be selected.

The selection is announced at least 1 week ahead, and the result is announced twice. The community has at least 1 week to challenge it in writing, and the Chair has 48 hours to answer a challenge. The second announcement officially starts the committee's term.
sections.eli5: Names are drawn by chance with a method anyone can check, and no company can take more than two of the ten seats. Then everyone gets a week to say if something looks wrong.

sections.title: How the Committee Works
sections.content:
Candidate selection is due within 3 months, at least two months before the First IETF, and confirmation within 1 month, at least one month before it. The Chair sets milestones and a voting mechanism. A candidate selection vote needs a quorum of at least 7 voting volunteers; at other times a quorum is at least 75% of members.

Anyone in the IETF community may nominate anyone, including themselves. Nominees must consent in writing before they can become candidates, and consent does not imply they will be chosen. The committee sends each confirming body a single candidate per open position, with testimony on how the candidate meets the qualifications. Rejected candidates and nominees are told before confirmed candidates are announced.

The committee may keep an archive of its information, for no longer than its term, to help with mid-term vacancies. Anything not otherwise specified is at the committee's discretion.
sections.eli5: The committee keeps to a calendar, asks everyone for ideas, checks that each person is willing, and tells people the news in the right order so nobody learns by surprise.

sections.title: Disputes and Recalls
sections.content:
Process disputes are first resolved inside the committee. If that fails, a written request goes to the Internet Society President, who appoints an arbiter (self-appointment is allowed). The result is final and binding, with no appeal, and the process should finish within two weeks. Meanwhile the committee must not submit candidates to a confirming body.

To recall a sitting IAB or IESG member, at least 20 members of the IETF community who qualify to be voting members of a nominating committee must send a signed petition to the Internet Society President, with no more than two signatories sharing an affiliation. The President appoints a Recall Committee Chair but must not evaluate the request. The recall committee is formed and run like the Nominating Committee, without confirmation, and it must give the member a chance to submit a written statement and consult third parties. A 3/4 majority of those voting is required, and the seat is then filled under the mid-term vacancy rules.
sections.eli5: If someone thinks the process went wrong, a neutral referee decides and that is that. To remove a leader, at least 20 qualified people must ask, and then three out of four of a special group must agree.

sections.title: Confidentiality
sections.content:
Selection, confirmation and recall all involve investigating the qualifications and activities of people, which may reveal confidential or private information. Everyone who takes part must keep confidential anything not explicitly marked suitable for public release.

When the committee decides it must share such information with others, the sharing must be minimal and each person consulted must first commit to the same confidentiality rules as the committee.
sections.eli5: People talk about candidates behind closed doors, and anyone told a secret must promise to keep it.
